newsitem.title: USA: Will they or won't they? Market eyes the Fed.
newsitem.headline: Will they or won't they? Market eyes the Fed.

text.p: Wall Street basked in the glow of a record-setting week, but despite the new highs set by the Dow Jones industrial average and the S&P 500, the market still is focused squarely on Tuesday's Federal Reserve meeting.
Interest rates, an obsession on Wall Street because lower rates can heat up the economy and higher rates cool it down, have been the topic of debate for weeks amid conflicting ecoomic data.

Economists have been scrutinising employment and production figures and analysts poring over the words of Fed officials for clues as to whether the central bank will raise interest rates at Tuesday's meeting of its policy-setting Federal Open Market Committee.
In the latest Reuters poll, conducted Thursday, 16 of 30 economists surveyed said the FOMC would raise interest rates by one-quarter of a percentage point at its Sept. 24 meeting.
Thirteen economists said the Fed would leave rates unchanged and one predicted a move of half a percentage point.
Yet, even with attention so squarely fixed and opinion so divided on this Fed meeting, only lately has a second question come to be addressed: namely, what difference does it make?

Analysts generally expect little stock market fallout in the event of a modest increase in the federal funds rate -- the rate banks charge each other for overnight loans -- currently targeted at 5.25 percent.
"If the Fed raises by 25 basis points, that's already priced in the market," said Thom Brown, managing director of Rutherford Brown and Catherwood.
Likewise, a Fed vote to leave rates unchanged is only expected to provide a short-lived, modest boost.

"If there's no change, I think there will be a mild celebration," said Larry Wachtel, market analyst at Prudential Securities. "But people may construe the decision as deferring to political sensibilities because the presidential debate will only be about a week away."
Indeed, of the 13 respondents to the Reuter survey who predicted no rise in rates, seven forecast a Fed tightening in late November, just after the presidential elections.
But hopes that the Fed would leave interest rates alone at Tuesday's meeting sent the Dow to a record close last Monday.

The blue-chip index soared briefly through 5,900 points for the first time Monday, before closing at a record 5,889.20. After three losing sessions, the Dow closed 20.72 points higher on Friday at 5,888.46. For the week, the Dow rose 49.94 points.
The Standard & Poor's index of 500 stocks rose 4.02 to 687.02 on Friday, topping Monday's record close of 683.98. The index was up 6.48 on the week.
The Nasdaq Composite index rose 7.60 points to 1,219.69 Friday -- moving in fast on June 5's all-time high finish of 1,249.15. The index edged up 31.02 from last Friday.

On the surface, the outlook for higher interest rates would seem to present a problem for the stock market, which clearly favours lower rates. However, the jitters about the fallout of a Fed move appear tamered than in recent past.

One reason is that the market is devoid of the speculative fervor that fuelled a fierce rally in small capitalisation stocks early in the year. By most indicators, smaller-cap stocks have yet to recoup their losses from the July correction.
Another is that recent data have delivered mixed signals about the state of the economy and inflation.
Despite a steep decline in the nation's unemployment rate and robust wage growth, companies have shown no ability to translate higher labour costs into price increases.
Until a clearer sign emerges on the inflation front, analysts do not really expect Tuesday's outcome to settle anything at all.
"I don't want to make the (meeting on the) 24th the be-all and end-all," Wachtel said, "because everybody realises this is a work in progress."
